Lifting prescribed identifications through localization

When using the universal property of a localization, it can matter which identification is obtained after restriction. Merely identifying the two extended functors does not compute the image of that identification. This note records the stronger calculation used in the formalization. Assume the Chapter 1 mapping-anima and pullback structures.

Supplementary Lemma 1. Let \(r\colon B\to C\) and suppose \(r^*\colon \Map (C,D)\to \Map (B,D)\) is an embedding. For functors \(f,g\colon C\to D\) and a specified identification \(\alpha \colon fr=gr\), there is an identification \(\widetilde \alpha \colon f=g\) with a specified higher identification \[ \widetilde \alpha |_r=\alpha . \]

Proof idea

Name \(f\) and \(g\) in \(\Map (C,D)\). Move \(\alpha \) across the comparisons between restriction of their names and names of their restrictions. The embedding \(r^*\) induces an equivalence of identification animae, so the resulting identification lifts with its prescribed image. Decode the lift and transport its endpoints back to \(f,g\).

The computation law for this decoding, together with its compatibility with restriction, proves the displayed image formula. The final endpoint transports are essential: the lifted identification initially has the decoded named functors as its endpoints. See also Decoding mapping animae and restriction. □

Supplementary Corollary 2. Let \(l\colon C\to L\) be a localization at a collection \(W\), in the setting of the book’s localization definition. For every target \(D\), restriction \(\Map (L,D)\to \Map (C,D)\) is an embedding. Consequently every specified identification between the restrictions of two functors \(L\to D\) lifts as in Supplementary Lemma 1.

Proof idea

Restriction factors through the equivalence \(\Map (L,D)\iso \Map ^W(C,D)\) and the inclusion of this subanima in \(\Map (C,D)\). A composite of an equivalence and an embedding is an embedding. The ordinary restriction map need not be an equivalence: its image consists of functors inverting \(W\). □

Supplementary Lemma 3. If \(r^*\colon \Map (C,D)\to \Map (B,D)\) is an equivalence, then for \(\alpha ,\beta \colon f=g\), an identification \(\alpha |_r=\beta |_r\) induces an identification \(\alpha =\beta \).

Proof idea

Encode \(\alpha \) and \(\beta \) as identifications between the names of \(f\) and \(g\). Naturality of decoding turns the hypothesis into an identification of their restricted encodings. Reflect through the induced equivalence of identification animae, decode, and cancel the endpoint comparisons. The equivalence hypothesis is the one used by this higher-reflection declaration. □

These two levels of calculation occur in preservation of pushouts by geometric realization. When reconstructing a cocone through restriction equivalences, first lift the legs and then lift the specified matching with Supplementary Lemma 1. For a comparison of cocones, lift both leg comparisons with prescribed images. Its matching equation can then be checked after restriction and reflected by Supplementary Lemma 3. Thus the comparison retains the whole cocone. The same distinction is useful when reading the uniqueness exercise for localizations.
